entries.original_title: Sequential congruency effects reveal differences in disengagement of attention for monolingual and bilingual young adults
entries.original_authors: Grundy, J; Chung-Fat-Yim, A; Friesen, D; Mak, L; Bialystok, E
entries.description: Grundy et al. claimed that monolingual and bilingual adults did not differ in their conventional flanker congruency effects.
entries.citation_sentence: Following this line of reasoning, Grundy et al. (2017) administered an Eriksen flanker task to groups of monolingual and bilingual adults.
entries.notes: The original reported this null conventional-effect finding, and the replication also found no group difference. This entry is secondary to the paper's main replication of the sequential congruency effect.

entries.original_title: Sequential congruency effects reveal differences in disengagement of attention for monolingual and bilingual young adults
entries.original_authors: Grundy, J; Chung-Fat-Yim, A; Friesen, D; Mak, L; Bialystok, E
entries.description: Grundy et al. claimed that bilingual adults showed smaller sequential congruency effects than monolingual adults.
entries.citation_sentence: One recent study, for example, reported smaller sequential congruency effects for bilingual compared to monolingual adults (Grundy et al., 2017).
entries.notes: The replication found no difference between monolingual and bilingual adults in sequential congruency effects and explicitly described its findings as inconsistent with the prior claim.
